I’m hiring: Legal Manager (Capital Markets & M&A) at Astra ⚖️
I recently joined Astra Enterprise (SET: ASTR) as Head of HR. Astra used to be DV8. It’s listed on Thailand’s mai market, and it’s changing from a media business into a digital asset company serving Thailand and Asia, with a focus on custody, treasury and financial services infrastructure.
We grow largely by buying and investing in other companies, so legal work is central to the business. That’s why this role matters so much.
📍 Bangkok | Hybrid | Full-time
What you’ll do
→ Run the legal side of acquisitions, JVs and strategic investments, from term sheet to closing and integration
→ Draft, review and negotiate SPAs, SHAs, subscription agreements and MOUs
→ Plan legal due diligence, manage external counsel, and turn findings into clear risks and contract protections
→ Advise on SET and SEC rules for listed companies: material transactions, connected transactions and disclosure
→ Build contract templates and playbooks for the business
→ Use AI and legal tech in your daily work, and help the team work faster and better
What we’re looking for
✔ LL.B., with 5–7 years’ post-qualification experience in corporate and M&A work (law firm, in-house, or both)
✔ Strong drafting: precise defined terms, clear structure, and a good sense of how clauses work together
✔ Good working knowledge of the rules for listed companies
✔ Ability to draft and negotiate in English with international counterparties
✔ Real interest in AI and new technology, not just using it
✔ Comfortable with ambiguity, proactive, and happy to take ownership
Nice to have
Experience at an international law firm
Knowledge of Thai digital asset regulation (we’ll help you learn)
Experience with cross-border deals or regulated financial services
An LL.M. or other postgraduate legal qualification
To be honest, this isn’t a role where you review the same contracts every day. You’ll help build new businesses from the start, work closely with leadership, and see live deals and new regulation happening in the digital asset market.

914 #legaloperations job postings (Oct). 629 different job titles.

Are we watching Legal Ops become more specialized, or more fragmented?

We reviewed 914 job postings from 648 employers for our Legal Operations Job Market Report

Three findings stood out to me

1. Generalists aren't the whole story
Only 23% of the postings were generalist roles. E-billing and bill review accounted for another 23%, while CLM and contracts operations represented 21%

Employers aren't just looking for someone to run Legal Ops. Many are hiring people to own specific parts of the function

2. Legal Engineering & AI are here
We identified 123 postings (13.5%) in legal engineering and AI transformation
Some of these roles look quite different from traditional Legal Ops. 

These roles emphasize building, integrating and automating how legal work gets done

3. Everyone wants experience. Who's developing it?
75% of the postings were mid-level or senior/manager roles.. only 14% were entry-level

That was perhaps my biggest takeaway

If employers are predominantly hiring people who already have experience, where are we creating opportunities for the next generation to develop that experience? 

...we will be keeping an eye on this trend.. see if this is seasonal or a point in time kind of observation

I also wonder whether we're making Legal Ops unnecessarily difficult to navigate with so many job titles and specializations

The function is complex and increasingly specialized in the roles employers are advertising... the question is whether the career paths, training and organizational structures are keeping up...

A quick note on methodology: I'm grateful to Señor AI and the incredible human brain power who collaborated with it.. hmm.. actually vice versa... special thanks to Imran and Hassan. It made it possible to go from a business question and hypothesis to a research dataset and directional findings in a relatively short time

This wasn't planned to be a peer-reviewed study or a comprehensive view of the market, but it gave us a useful starting point for understanding where Legal Ops hiring may be heading.. so we thought we'd share

... and like I mentioned, we will be keeping an eye on how the trends develop

We published the full report, including hiring disciplines, seniority, salary ranges and locations, with plans to update it quarterly

🌐 https://lnkd.in/gAyqZy6j

The Maldives could also gain housing, public revenue and US dollar inflows. Those gains need weighing against imported inputs, infrastructure costs and environmental impacts. Housing benefits depend on delivery, prices and eligibility; sales of premium residences alone do not prove improved affordability.

For Eagle Hills, successful local partnerships could support delivery, property sales, development returns and its regional brand. These are potential gains for a UAE-based private company, not established benefits to the UAE government.

Estimated development value is not committed financing. The practical test is published contract terms, funding, local purchasing and hiring results, alongside enforceable infrastructure and environmental responsibilities.

In the early ’80s, Van Halen’s concert rider had a clause about a bowl of M&Ms with every brown one removed.
 
It sounds like rock star excess. It was really a safety check. The rider was full of technical requirements for a very heavy stage setup, and if the band found brown M&Ms backstage, they knew the promoter hadn’t read the contract closely. So they’d go back and check everything else.
 
In 2009, Twilio wrote about using the same idea in hiring. Ask applicants for one small, specific thing with their cover letter, and you find out right away who read the posting.
 
Recently a company hid an instruction near the bottom of a content strategist posting asking applicants to include a frog poem. A person reading the posting would never see it. An AI that was handed the posting to write the application would see it and follow it.
 
For 40 years, this test caught people who didn’t read.
 
Now the AI does the reading, and the test catches the person who handed it off.
 
So I’m curious. Does anyone out there still read the whole job posting themselves? Or have we all quietly stopped?

Open-systems procurement frameworks such as MOSA and MOSABw favour a vendor-neutral software layer. But Helsing, Anduril and Shield AI all compete in autonomy, and Europe's defence start-ups are still short of government customers. The next test is whether SE3's Bundeswehr and Ukraine work turns into larger, repeat orders.

One key takeaway following 2 days at Going Global Live Business Show. 

The most important change at The Business Show London wasn’t a product. It was a word: “partner.”
Two days at ExCeL, with 25,000 visitors expected and 500 exhibitors and around 200 speakers. Going Global Live, the UK’s largest exhibition for international expansion, ran alongside.

The pitch on the floor has shifted completely. Accountants now call themselves “strategic partners in growth.” Funding brokers tell founders to “get clear, get ready.” HR outsourcing and EOR providers lay out whole stacks for expansion. .

Regardless of the industry, every company has stopped selling a service or a product, and started selling a stake in the founder’s growth.

To me, the reason is obvious. A founder expanding into new markets can’t manage twelve vendors. Accounting, funding, hiring and compliance across jurisdictions, pipeline, AI: each one has its own contract, its own onboarding and its own reporting. The hours that should be dedicated to  growth are spent on coordination.

So the winning model is a team of partners, orchestrated around one growth plan.
In that team, #AI is just another partner. It’s the one that takes the repeatable work, with no onboarding and no sick days. 

One case from the keynote stage that stuck with me: a five-site dental group implemented an AI analyst to score every patient call, which no team had the hours to do by hand. The agent had identified over £573 thousands of missed revenue in only 2 months. Despite of the fact that AI agent found the leak, the people were the ones who still had to decide what to fix.

This new division of labour is another takeaway from this year’s show - the new normal after the AI noise is over now, then comes the time for some companies to stand out.
Partners and AI carry the routine. The founder carries the growth decisions: which market, which buyer, which hire, which deal. Whereas the rest of the team pushes forward what may cripple growth: the hesitant buyer, the negotiation, the decision on which market to enter next. Whether AI is involved or not, the order is the same: find the leak, automate what drains hours, and give those hours to what only people can do.

That’s the lesson I took from the whole floor! 
Don’t start with the tool - as the tool helps automate what’s easy. Companies that start with the objective - to spot and eliminatel the leak automate what pays, and free their people for what only humans do. 

Where is your growth system leaking, and how many hours would it take a human to find out?

And one more thing. Yeah, it’s freezing in London today ;)

Legal groundwork is often the cheapest insurance an AI startup will ever buy. The relationship with a good lawyer also compounds in value the longer it runs, so it's worth starting early.

Founders put most of their early capital into the idea and the product. Legal decisions get pushed aside, and that's where expensive problems start. Here's what I'd be thinking about from day one:

	1.	Who owns what. Every founder, contractor, and early hire should sign an IP assignment agreement that transfers code, models, and datasets to the company before they touch the product. Co-founders also need clear equity vesting, because a departing founder holding unvested shares is a common way early companies stall.

	2.	Where your training data came from. Document the source, license, and terms of every dataset, scraped source, and third-party API you use. Many terms of service restrict training or commercial use, and fixing that exposure after customers and investors are reviewing your company is far harder than getting it right early.

	3.	What happens when the model is wrong. Wrong, biased, or harmful outputs are inevitable. Customer contracts should define warranties, indemnities, and liability caps that match what your product can actually guarantee. Vague promises about accuracy are a frequent source of disputes.

	4.	Regulation that already applies. The EU AI Act, U.S. state AI laws, GDPR, CCPA, and sector rules in healthcare, finance, and hiring are either in force or arriving fast. A lawyer who knows this landscape can tell you which obligations apply to your use case before you build the wrong thing.

	5.	Privacy and data commitments. Decide early whether you'll train on customer data, how long you'll keep it, and whether users can opt out. These choices are far easier to make before they become promises you've already made.

	6.	Entity structure and fundraising. The right entity, cap table, and standard financing documents keep future rounds from requiring expensive cleanup. A lawyer who has closed many startup financings can help you avoid terms that scare investors away.

The relationship itself matters too. A firm that knows your company from incorporation can spot patterns, like the same data-licensing question coming up across three customers, and solve it once. When a dispute or acquisition arises, they already know your history, which saves time and money. Many startup-focused firms offer reduced or deferred fees for early companies, so the cost of starting is often lower than founders expect.

Legal counsel is not a cost to minimize. It's an early investment in your company's ability to raise money, sign large customers, and avoid expensive rework. The founders who treat it that way often find a good lawyer is one of the highest-return relationships they build.

If you're an AI founder, what legal issue cost you the most time early on? I'd like to hear it.

The $400,000 Question: Does Your Company Really Need a Full-Time General Counsel?

According to the Association of Corporate Counsel's 2025 compensation survey, median annual cash compensation for a General Counsel or Chief Legal Officer is approximately $410,000. That's before benefits, payroll taxes, and other employment costs.

For many growing businesses, that's a substantial investment.

But here's the more important question:

Does your company need a full-time general counsel, or does it need access to the experience and judgment of one?

Those aren't necessarily the same thing.

Today's businesses face increasingly complex commercial agreements, technology and licensing arrangements, data privacy and AI challenges, corporate governance issues, and strategic transactions.

They need sophisticated legal advice. But they may not need 40 hours of it every week.
Before becoming an attorney, I spent seven years in business development. That experience fundamentally shaped how I practice law.

A contract isn't simply a collection of legal provisions. It's a commercial relationship. A negotiation isn't about winning every point. It's about getting the deal done while protecting the business.

Over the years, I've advised companies on complex transactions, strategic partnerships, technology, data, and corporate matters.

And I've learned that the most valuable legal advice often isn't explaining what the law permits. It's understanding what the business is trying to accomplish and finding a practical way to get there.

That's where the outside general counsel model makes sense.

Companies can access experienced, business-minded legal counsel without the fixed costs of a full-time executive.

More importantly, they gain an ongoing strategic partner who understands their business, anticipates problems, and helps management make better decisions.

For some companies, hiring a full-time general counsel is absolutely the right investment.

For others, particularly growing and middle-market businesses, there's a more efficient way.

The goal isn't to spend less on legal advice. It's to get the right experience, at the right time, at a cost that makes sense.

Because the value of a general counsel isn't measured by hours spent in the office.

It's measured by the decisions they help a business make.

You don't need a team of twenty engineers anymore to build a complex crypto trading system.

The old way meant hiring a team and managing months of sprints.

Agent orchestration changes that math completely.

With today's agent tools, one founder can run a whole set of specialized agents.

One agent watches smart contract vulnerability databases. Another writes unit tests for Solana program instructions. A third keeps refactoring the Rust code to cut gas, and a fourth reads Telegram and X data for sentiment shifts.

What makes this work is clear boundaries.

Never give one prompt the job of "build a trading bot."

Split the work into small tasks with explicit inputs and outputs. Each one gets its own prompt and an automated check that says pass or fail.

When an agent's code fails a test, the compiler output goes straight back into its context window. It fixes its own code in a loop, the same way CI would.

🎯 Split your AI coding workflow into isolated tasks, each with a prompt spec and automated tests that feed errors back to the agent.

⏳ Duration: Contract
🌎 Work Authorization: H1B | USC | H4 EAD | TN
📩 rani.p@xforiatech.com

Role Overview:
We are looking for an experienced Lead AI Conversational Data Engineer with a strong Data Engineering background and 3+ years of hands-on experience in Conversational AI, Agentic AI, or Generative AI.
The ideal candidate will build customer-specific synthetic datasets and end-to-end RAG/knowledge pipelines to support Conversational AI (CCAI), voice, and chat deployments. The role focuses on generating realistic, privacy-safe synthetic data and developing reusable, automated data generation and ingestion pipelines across GCP and AWS.
Key Responsibilities:
Design and develop customer-specific synthetic conversation datasets for voice and chat.
Generate CCAI training and evaluation dialogues, FAQs, knowledge-base articles, and structured entity data.
Build and maintain end-to-end RAG and knowledge ingestion pipelines.
Prepare, index, and evaluate knowledge corpora for retrieval-based applications.
Work with customer intents, entities, languages, document types, and conversational edge cases.
Validate synthetic data quality, diversity, coverage, and PII safety.
Automate reusable data generation, ingestion, and index-refresh pipelines.
Work with Conversational AI Platform and DevOps teams to support customer deployments.
Required Skills:
Strong Data Engineering experience.
3+ years of hands-on experience in Conversational AI / Agentic AI / Generative AI.
Synthetic Data Generation and LLM-assisted data generation.
RAG, Knowledge Pipelines, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation.
Conversational data, voice/chat transcripts, and CCAI training data.
GCP services, BigQuery, AWS, and S3.
Data ingestion, indexing, document stores, and data quality validation.
Strong understanding of data privacy and PII protection.

📍 Location: Chicago, IL (First Preference) | Remote candidates can be considered

🔹 Key Responsibilities:
Design and develop GenAI-powered applications.
Build and integrate LLM-based solutions using APIs and AI frameworks.
Develop RAG pipelines and work with vector databases.
Implement prompt engineering and context management.
Integrate AI solutions with enterprise applications and backend systems.
Optimize AI solutions for performance, scalability, and accuracy.

🔹 Required Technical Skills:
Strong Python programming experience.
Hands-on experience with Generative AI and LLMs.
LangChain or LlamaIndex.
Strong knowledge of Prompt Engineering and RAG.
Vector Databases: Pinecone, FAISS, ChromaDB.
REST APIs and cloud platforms (AWS/Azure/GCP).
AI model deployment experience.

🔹 Preferred Skills:
Agentic AI and AI Agents.
Fine-tuning, Embeddings, and Model Evaluation.
Docker, Kubernetes, and CI/CD.

📩 Interested candidates: Please share your updated resume at Rajat3@votoconsulting.com

🤝 Referrals are highly appreciated!
